It doesn’t matter if I do or if I don’t. I think maybe something in New York is waiting on me now.
When you were coming up, you never said, “I want to be the best” or whatever?
No.
You never had that kind of . . .
No
You just knew that you were going to be the best. You didn’t have to say it, right?
I didn’t know.
Yes you did.
But I have to be the best that I can do. I don’t know if it’s the best.

I’ll say for you: you have been the best, Melba. You’ve been a guiding light for a lot of people, including me, and I want to ask you what advice you would have for some of the young girls coming along who are musicians? What advice would you give them?

Study. Go to school and learn everything that you can in school, and don’t stop there. Get what you can out of school, jamming and everything. It’s about learning and about doing. It’s hard now. It’s still hard for girls, but . . .
But they still won’t have it as hard as you did.
Oh no.
Was there any particular school that you think that they could go to that would really qualify to do what you said, go and learn, not just . . .

[cannot recall any school to recommend.] But wherever they go to school, college and stuff, make them teach you as much as they know how. And go on, like we did at nighttime – go to other places and get some knowledge there.

And do you think that they should pick someone as their model – not particularly role model, but as a model that they would listen to, like I’ve heard Charli Persip say he went to whatever the college was that he went to, but he finished from the Gillespie University. You know what I’m saying?

Yeah, I would say that. Yes indeed. Get someone that you like to have. Horn players, get someone to take a pattern off of. Everything that’s out there, they can have somebody older to pattern off of . . .
Yeah, they need someone to latch onto.
. . . and maybe after so many years of that, you can go and get someone else to . . .

Yeah, right. Move on up to the modern day, or whatever. Do you find that they’re more – the children and young kids coming up, male and female, on the East Coast, seem to be the ones who reach back in – I mean who reach up and take a role model’s hand and try to pattern themselves at the beginning, until they get where they can walk on their – in their own shoes, and then they still want to
recognize where they came from? Because out here on the West Coast I don’t seem to find that.
I don’t see where that’s happening out here.
No, I don’t either.
But East Coast . . .
I wonder why that is.
I don’t know, because you know better than me. I don’t get around too much, and I wouldn’t get around if I was able to. I would be back in New York.
You wouldn’t even be here, Melba.
I would come here on occasions.

But that bothers me, that the kids – they’re not – you know what. It seems like they think the music starts and ends with them, that they – nobody was here before them, so they don’t have to recognize – I really don’t hear kids doing that.
I don’t know what these kids are doing.
But those schools that you helped organize and stuff like that, the kids wanted to learn, and they came there to learn, and they did learn, because you guys were teaching them.
Yeah. Back there. In the West Indies, St. Lucia, everywhere but here.

Right. Isn’t that funny? In Japan, in Europe. But it’s so funny that we – on this Coast, we cannot get it together, as far as I can see. And you’re not going to stick around and try and help us get it together.
I’ve been here six, seven years or something. I’m going to go back there and get a new start or something.

“I’m going to change my way of living. If that ain’t enough, I’m going to change the way I strut my stuff.” Because Melba you’ve really overcome the stroke that you had. I think you’ve made a long stride, bettering yourself to overcome that, and I think when you go back East, you’ll do even greater, because like you said, those people back – they recognize you for who you are back there.
I was afraid to go out and see everybody – anybody, until six months ago or something like that, because . . .
You’d sit in this room.
. . . I didn’t want them to gloat over me or something.
Feel sorry for you and then pity you and all those kinds of things.
Yeah, but it’s not like that.
But see it’s your attitude that keeps it from being that way. You don’t have that kind of attitude so you not going to get . . .
No.
. . . so you won’t get that kind of a treatment from people.
I know that.
Because it’s like Matt says, you’ve taken it – your stroke in stride. I know a lot of people who’ve had it, and they’ve had that attitude, “Oh, woe is me.”
I must have done that when I first . . .
When you first had it. Sure, but farther on down the road . . .
Yeah, I got to get on up.
You got to turn [?] loose. But what did you think after you had your stroke? What did you think? Did you think you would be able to play again? What?
You don’t think. It’s a long time before you can think. You learn how to eat with . . .
It’s the learning process all over?
Yeah, but I think Randy pushed me along.
Before you even – before you came out here?
Oh yeah.
But when you got here, your mother was still alive. Did she push you too?
Oh yeah, but Randy helped me to get started writing, and so I’m doing it. I’m not writing as fast and all of that as I . . .
The quality is there though, Melba.
. . . I used to, but maybe I’ll get that back in New York, but I don’t have to go as fast, anyway.

If they want you to write fast, say, “You better get somebody else. If you want something good, then you take me.” What about after your stroke and then you begin to move around and so forth? What did you think about not being able to play your horn? Or did you think about it?
No. The horn was stolen.
Oh, that’s right.
